items.title: Money M
items.question: In the classic puzzle SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, each letter is a distinct digit. Which digit does M stand for?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. A carry into a new leading column can only be one, which pins the letter M.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. The leading digit of the sum must come from a single carry, so it is forced.
items.lessonContent:
Leading digits reveal carries.
A new column can only carry one.
Constraints force values before guessing.
Start from the most restricted column.
Share this: solve a letter puzzle by starting where a value is forced.

items.title: Money O
items.question: In SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, which digit represents the letter O?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 0. Once other digits are placed, only zero remains for this letter.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 0. The puzzle's constraints leave this letter with the one unused digit.
items.lessonContent:
Elimination assigns remaining values.
Place the forced digits first.
The leftovers often fit one slot.
Track which digits are already used.
Share this: finish a puzzle by elimination once constraints narrow the options.

items.title: Money Y
items.question: In SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, the units column decides the last letter. What value does Y take?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. The units column forces the value once the other digits are fixed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Working column by column from the right settles this letter last.
items.lessonContent:
Columns resolve from the right.
The units column often fixes a digit.
Proceed stepwise with carries.
Verify the whole sum afterward.
Share this: solve one column at a time and carry forward.

items.title: Money D
items.question: In SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, which digit does D represent?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 7. The units interaction with the carry forces this value.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7. Applying the carry rules to the rightmost column identifies it.
items.lessonContent:
Carries link neighbouring columns.
Use one column to constrain the next.
Fix digits in dependency order.
Recheck each carry.
Share this: trace how a carry from one column shapes another.

items.title: Money E
items.question: In that same sum, the letter E appears twice. What digit must it hold?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 5. The tens and hundreds columns together force this digit.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. This letter appears twice, so both occurrences must agree.
items.lessonContent:
Repeated letters must match.
One letter, two positions, one value.
Use consistency as a constraint.
Check every occurrence.

items.title: Four F
items.question: In TWO plus TWO equals FOUR, which digit does F represent?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. The extra leading digit of the sum comes from carrying, so it must be one.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. A sum one digit longer than its addends always starts with the carry.
items.lessonContent:
Longer sums begin with a carry.
The leading digit of a new column is one.
Identify where padding appears.
Use it to start solving.
Share this: note when a sum gains digit length and why.

items.title: Four O
items.question: In TWO plus TWO equals FOUR, O appears in both the addend and the sum. Which digit satisfies both?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 4. Doubling the tens digit with its carry yields this value in the result.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. The letter appears in both addend and sum, so both must match.
items.lessonContent:
Shared letters constrain both sides.
Doubling produces carries to track.
Use equality across positions.
Verify with the final sum.
Share this: use a symbol appearing twice to narrow the digits.

items.title: Four U
items.question: In TWO plus TWO equals FOUR, the hundreds column with its carry fixes one letter. Which digit does U take?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 6. The hundreds column, including its carry, fixes this digit.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Working from the carries inward identifies the value.
items.lessonContent:
Carries pass leftward.
Each column includes the carry from the right.
Solve in order of dependency.
Confirm the arithmetic.
Share this: follow a carry through two adjacent columns.

items.title: Four R
items.question: In TWO plus TWO equals FOUR, the units column doubles and carries. What digit lands in R's place?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 8. The units column doubles the ones digit and carries into the next.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Doubling a ones digit produces the final place of the sum.
items.lessonContent:
The units place is fixed first.
Doubling there sets the final digit.
Carry the extra leftward.
Keep the columns aligned.
Share this: compute the units place of a doubled number first.

items.title: Four T
items.question: In TWO plus TWO equals FOUR, the addend's leading digit comes from the carries. Which digit is T?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 7. The leading digit of the addend is fixed by the carries running through the columns.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7. Solving from the right constraints propagates to the leading place.
items.lessonContent:
Constraints propagate from right to left.
Leading digits depend on carries.
Solve the small columns first.
Then read off the front.

items.title: Four W
items.question: In TWO plus TWO equals FOUR, once the other letters are fixed one digit remains for W. Which is it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Once the neighbouring digit is known, the remaining value follows from the column sum.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. The column arithmetic leaves one digit that satisfies all constraints.
items.lessonContent:
One remaining value satisfies the column.
Use the sum to find it.
Check that distinct letters keep distinct digits.
Verify the complete equation.

items.title: Letter Value
items.question: In a cryptarithm, what does each distinct letter stand for?
choices: A whole number of any size
items.correctExplanation: Right. Each letter maps to one digit, and different letters map to different digits.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a distinct digit. This one-to-one mapping is what makes the puzzle solvable by elimination.
items.lessonContent:
Letter puzzles encode digits one-to-one.
Distinctness creates constraints.
Elimination does the heavy lifting.
Start from the tightest restriction.
Share this: solve a substitution puzzle by listing what each symbol cannot be.

items.title: No Sharing
items.question: May two different letters in a standard cryptarithm represent the same digit?
choices: The mapping is one to one
items.correctAnswer: The mapping is one to one
items.correctExplanation: Right. The mapping is one-to-one, so distinct letters take distinct values.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the mapping is one to one. Allowing sharing would make the puzzle ambiguous and unsolvable by unique reasoning.
items.lessonContent:
One-to-one mappings keep puzzles determinate.
Rules create the constraints that enable solving.
Ambiguity usually signals a broken premise.
Check assumptions before solving.
Share this: identify one puzzle whose rule prevents ambiguity.

items.title: No Leading Zero
items.question: In a cryptarithm, may the leading letter of a multi-digit number be zero?
items.correctExplanation: Right. A leading zero would make a number shorter than written, breaking the puzzle's structure.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a leading zero is disallowed. Disallowing it preserves the number of digits in each term.
items.lessonContent:
Conventions define valid puzzles.
Leading zeros would change a number's length.
Rules preserve the intended structure.
Apply conventions consistently.
Share this: note why one standard convention exists.

items.title: Reverse Sum
items.question: For the puzzle AB plus BA equals 121 with distinct digits, what must A plus B equal?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 11. A number plus its reverse equals eleven times the digit sum.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 11. Dividing the total by eleven reveals the sum of the two digits.
items.lessonContent:
Reversing digits scales by eleven.
Recognise the pattern to divide quickly.
Extract a hidden quantity from a total.
Use structure before trial.

items.title: Biggest Carry
items.question: What is the largest carry possible from adding a single column in base ten?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Two digits plus a carry reach at most nineteen, so the carry out is one.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Larger carries cannot occur when adding only two digits per column.
items.lessonContent:
Column addition bounds the carry.
Two digits cap the sum below twenty.
Carries are small, not arbitrary.
Use bounds to limit possibilities.
Share this: find the maximum carry for one column under a stated rule.

items.title: Multiple Of
items.question: Any two-digit number added to its reverse gives a result that is always a multiple of what?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 11. The sum equals eleven times the sum of the two digits.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 11. This fixed factor is why such sums are easy to recognise.
items.lessonContent:
Hidden factors follow from place value.
Reversal scales the digit sum.
Spot structure to factor quickly.
Use patterns as shortcuts.

items.title: Money N
items.question: In SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, which value does N hold?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 6. The hundreds and thousands columns together force this digit.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Solving the carries in order pins the value down.
items.lessonContent:
Values emerge from interacting columns.
Solve the most constrained letter first.
Use each result to narrow the rest.
Check the whole sum at the end.

items.title: Money S
items.question: In SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, the thousands column with its carry forces the leading letter. Which digit is S?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 9. The thousand column sum with its carry forces the largest digit here.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. The carry into the ten-thousands place determines this leading value.
items.lessonContent:
Leading digits are constrained by carries.
High values often appear at the front.
Work from the restricted columns.
Confirm with the full addition.

items.title: Money Total
items.question: In SEND plus MORE equals MONEY, what number does the word MONEY stand for?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 10652. With SEND as 9567 and MORE as 1085, the sum is 10652.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10652. Reconstructing the addends digit by digit makes the total verifiable.
items.lessonContent:
Completed puzzles yield checkable totals.
Verify by substituting every letter.
A full sum confirms each assignment.
Check the arithmetic at the end.

items.title: Shared Digit
items.question: If two different letters in a valid cryptarithm were assigned the same digit, the puzzle would become what?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Shared digits break the one-to-one rule and allow multiple solutions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ambiguous. The distinctness rule exists precisely to guarantee a unique decoding.
items.lessonContent:
Rules preserve unique solutions.
Breaking a rule invites multiple answers.
Ambiguity undermines puzzle design.
Check premises before solving.
Share this: find one constraint that keeps a puzzle's answer unique.

items.title: Letter Limit
items.question: At most how many distinct letters can a base-ten cryptarithm use?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 10. There are only ten digits, and each letter needs a distinct one.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. The alphabet's size is irrelevant; the digit supply is the binding limit.
items.lessonContent:
Supply bounds possible mappings.
Count the available values.
Do not confuse symbols with resources.
Find the real constraint.
Share this: identify the true limit on a substitution scheme.

items.title: Avoided Letters
items.question: Why are letters such as O and I sometimes avoided in cryptarithms?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Their shapes can be confused with zero and one, which muddles the notation.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is they resemble digits. Clarity matters when letters stand in for numbers.
items.lessonContent:
Notation should avoid ambiguity.
Similar shapes invite misreading.
Design choices reduce errors.
Choose clear symbols.

items.title: Puzzle Name
items.question: What is the standard name for a letter-arithmetic puzzle where letters stand for digits?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The name covers puzzles where words encode a hidden arithmetic equation.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a cryptarithm. The other terms describe letter arrangements, not digit substitutions.
items.lessonContent:
Names organise a family of puzzles.
Learn the term to find resources.
Distinguish similar-sounding forms.
Use precise vocabulary.

items.title: Eleven Letters
items.question: Why can a standard cryptarithm not use eleven distinct letters in base ten?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Ten digits cannot be assigned distinctly to eleven letters.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is not enough digits. The distinctness rule makes eleven letters impossible in base ten.
items.lessonContent:
Resource limits bound assignments.
Count symbols against available values.
Test a scheme against its constraints.
Recognise impossible cases early.
